summary.short: Bill adding Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 149B: employers and their vendors must give notice of worker data collection, electronic monitoring and automated decision systems, limit their use, and complete impact assessments. Enforced by the Attorney General and worker civil actions. Effective date not stated.
summary.long: Bill that would insert a new Chapter 149B into the General Laws, covering employers and their vendors for workplaces in Massachusetts, and state workers as specified in section 6. It defines worker data, electronic monitoring and automated decision systems (ADS). Employers must give workers notice of worker data collection, electronic monitoring and ADS use, and send notices to the Department of Labor & Workforce Development. Data collection is limited to listed purposes and the least invasive means; sale or licensing of worker data is barred. Electronic monitoring is restricted, including facial, gait and emotion recognition, monitoring of off-duty workers and private areas, and monitoring that prevents rest breaks or exercise of legal rights. ADS may not be solely relied on for hiring, promotion, termination, discipline or wages, and certain ADS uses are prohibited. Employers must complete independent impact assessments before using ADS or worker information systems, submit them to the Department, and publish summaries; the Department may require changes or bar use. Employers are jointly and severally liable for vendors. Workers and the Attorney General may sue for injunctive relief and civil penalties set in section 6(c). Department regulations are due by January 1, 2025. Effective date not stated.

notes: Bill text (introduced stage, as provided); the version and date are not stated in the document. No legal_basis or enacted_by_bill relation is stated in the text. Internal inconsistencies: (1) two provisions are headed 'Section 6' (Enforcement; and state workers), and the definition of 'Worker' cites 'section 6' for state workers; (2) Sections 3C(c) and 4C(c) refer to a 'department of labor standards' and 4C(c) to its 'occupational safety and health statistics program', while 'Department' is defined as the department of labor & workforce development; (3) Section 6(c)(iv) penalises failure to submit an impact assessment under sections 5, 5A, 5B or 5C, but Section 5C is a dispute procedure. Section 3B(b)(ii) cites 'paragraph (1)', which does not exist in that section.

thresholds.note: No numeric cutoff changes legal treatment in the operative provisions. The numbers in the text are penalty amounts (Sec. 6(c), enforcement), procedural deadlines (Secs. 2(d), 3B, 4(a), 4B(c), 5B(e), 6(b)(i)-(ii), handled as events), and the workers-affected figure in the Sec. 3C(c) and Sec. 4C(b) summaries, which is a reporting item and not a scope or eligibility cutoff. The 'Employer', 'Worker' and 'Vendor' definitions contain no size or count threshold. The 'Additional purposes' and 'prohibited ADS' lists are delegated to the department without numeric values.
